claims.text: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a large caloric response under applied magnetic or pressure fields.
The untreated alloy has poor structural integrity and tends to crack.
The untreated alloy has a predominantly single-phase or otherwise brittle microstructure.
Controlling cooling rate or solidification kinetics will promote secondary-phase precipitation in the target alloy.
The precipitated secondary phase will be ductile.
The treatment will create a dual-phase microstructure in the target alloy.
The secondary phase will form a homogeneous network along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The secondary-phase network will impede crack propagation.
Strain partitioning and crack blunting by the ductile phase will reinforce the brittle matrix.
A dual-phase or precipitate-containing architecture can improve alloy strength.
The treated alloy will have greater compressive or tensile strength than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will have greater ductility and reduced cracking relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will preserve the intrinsic phase transformation responsible for the caloric response.
The treated alloy's entropy change or adiabatic temperature change will remain similar to that of the untreated alloy.
The intervention will remain effective during applied magnetic-field and pressure-field operation, temperature cycling, and compressive or tensile loading.
The intervention will be effective at both ambient and elevated operating temperatures.
The intervention introduces no rare-earth elements.

contradictions.description: The mechanism is framed as modification of solidification kinetics and cooling rate, but the conditions also permit a post-casting heat treatment, which cannot modify the already completed solidification kinetics. The hypothesis does not distinguish a solidification-stage treatment from a post-solidification anneal.
